H1.text: A welding torch with a blinding flame. A miner's lamp that runs on a stone and water. Mangoes that ripen far too fast.

H2.text: Three puzzles. One gas hides behind all of them.

H3.text: Diya sees it in the kitchen. Her grandmother opens a box of mangoes and finds a small grey stone inside.

H4.text: Grandmother throws the stone away. It gives off a gas when it gets wet. Using it on fruit is not allowed.

H5.text: That gas is ethyne. By the end, you will know why it has a triple bond, and why its hydrogen can leave.

P2.text: An alkyne is a hydrocarbon, made only of carbon and hydrogen, with one carbon carbon triple bond.

P3.text: Their general formula is C n H two n minus two.

P4.text: The first one is ethyne, C two H two. Its old name is acetylene.

P5.text: Next comes propyne, C three H four.

P6.text: With four carbons, the triple bond can sit at the end, in but one yne, or in the middle, in but two yne. These are position isomers.

S1.text: Let's build the triple bond on our molecule bench.

S2.text: Each carbon in ethyne is s p hybridised: two s p orbitals in a straight line, and two p orbitals left over.

S3.text: One s p orbital from each carbon overlaps head on. That makes one strong sigma bond.

S4.text: The other s p orbitals hold the hydrogens. So the molecule is a straight line, at one hundred and eighty degrees.

S5.text: Now the leftover p orbitals. The upright pair overlaps side by side. That is the first pi bond.

S6.text: The front and back pair also overlaps side by side. That is the second pi bond, at right angles to the first.

S7.text: The two pi clouds wrap the carbons like a tube. One sigma plus two pi makes the triple bond.

B1.text: Three bonds pull the carbons close: one hundred and twenty picometres, against one hundred and fifty four for a single bond.

B2.text: Its bond enthalpy is eight hundred and twenty three kilojoules per mole.

B3.text: Now the surprise. The hydrogen on a triple bond carbon is a little acidic. It can leave as a proton.

B4.text: Think of a tug of war. An s p carbon has fifty percent s character, so it holds the bond electrons close and tight.

B5.text: When a base pulls the hydrogen away, the electron pair stays behind on the carbon. Watch the arrow.

B6.text: Pause and think. Whose hydrogen leaves most easily: ethane, ethene, or ethyne?

B7.text: Ethyne! Its s p carbon has the most s character, so it holds the electrons best. Ethene comes next, then ethane.

D1.text: Now, how do we make ethyne? One link at a time.

D2.text: Link one. Heat limestone, calcium carbonate. It gives quicklime and carbon dioxide.

D3.text: Link two. Heat quicklime with coke, almost pure carbon. We get calcium carbide and carbon monoxide.

D4.text: Link three. Add water to calcium carbide. Out bubbles ethyne. This is the stone in the mango box.

D5.text: Link four. Start from a vicinal dihalide, with halogens on neighbouring carbons. Alcoholic K O H pulls off one H X.

D6.text: Link five. Sodamide pulls off the second H X. Now we have the triple bond.

T1.text: Remember this. One sigma, two pi, and an end hydrogen that can leave.

W1.text: Now, one worked example. What does propyne give with sodium, and with two molecules of H B r?

W2.text: Step one. Propyne has a hydrogen on its end triple bond carbon. So sodium replaces it, and hydrogen gas bubbles out.

W3.text: Step two. Pi bonds are weaker than sigma bonds, so alkynes add things across them.

W4.text: Step three. The first H B r adds by Markovnikov's rule. Hydrogen goes to the carbon that already has more hydrogens.

W5.text: Step four. So bromine lands on the middle carbon. We get two bromopropene.

W6.text: Step five. The second H B r adds the same way. Two two dibromopropane.

C2.text: Hydrogen with a platinum, palladium or nickel catalyst turns ethyne into ethene, then ethane.

C3.text: Reddish orange bromine in carbon tetrachloride loses its colour. That is a test for unsaturation.

C4.text: Water adds with mercury ions and acid at three hundred and thirty three kelvin. Propyne becomes propanone.

C5.text: Finally, pass ethyne through a red hot iron tube at eight hundred and seventy three kelvin. Three molecules join into a benzene ring.

X2.text: Students say every alkyne reacts with sodium and gives hydrogen gas, so but two yne must too.

X3.text: Wrong. Only terminal alkynes have a hydrogen on a triple bond carbon. But two yne has none there, so nothing happens.

E1.text: Where is this asked? Acidic alkynes, Markovnikov addition and the carbide method.

Q1.text: Exam level now. Compound X, C three H four, gives hydrogen gas with sodium. With water, mercury ions and acid, it gives Y. What is Y? Pause and solve.

A2.text: X gives hydrogen with sodium, so it is a terminal alkyne. C three H four is propyne.

A3.text: Water adds by Markovnikov's rule. The O H lands on the middle carbon and forms an enol.

A4.text: The enol shifts into a ketone, propanone. Propanal would need the O H on the end carbon.

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these three questions without help?

Y2.text: One. How many sigma and pi bonds are in a carbon carbon triple bond?

Y3.text: Two. Why is the hydrogen of ethyne more acidic than the hydrogen of ethane?

Y4.text: Three. What forms when calcium carbide meets water?

N1.text: Next time: why does benzene refuse to behave like it has three double bonds? We find out in benzene and aromaticity.
